newsitem.title: USA: USG grain terminal outage may dampen freight rates.
newsitem.headline: USG grain terminal outage may dampen freight rates.

text.p: The closure of one of the biggest grain terminals on the Mississippi River following a ship accident there last week may depress bulk freight rates, as excess tonnage builds up in the U.S. Gulf, shipping sources said.
Zen-Noh Grain Corp's Convent, Louisiana, corn loading facility remained shut on Tuesday, six days after a grain vessel crashed into one of the plant's four loading towers.

Regarded as one of the most efficient grain loading facilities in the U.S. Gulf, the Zen-Noh plant was capable of loading a 50,000-tonne grain vessel in about a day and a half, compared with an industry average of two and a half to three days, traders said.
The company had yet to say how long the facility would be closed, but industry sources said repairs could take anywhere from a few weeks to two months.
"There is no way that you can replace the loss of that house," said one shipbroker. "It will result in maybe 10 grain cargoes a month not getting shipped out of the U.S. Gulf."

Rates on Panamax shipments to the Far East have pulled back slightly in the past few days, with fixtures quoted at $25.25 per tonne on Tuesday, against $25.50 seen late last week. Brokers said further weakness was likely as the outage wears on.

"If it goes on for a month, there will be less cargo around for the vessels, so rates will go down," said a broker with an East Coast shipping firm. "It will probably have a downward effect rather than upward."
The Zen-Noh outage comes at a time when congestion of outbound cargoes in the U.S. Gulf was already on the rise.

In recent weeks, Canadian grain shippers, facing severe delays in the Pacific Northwest, have been forced to reroute trans-Pacific grain shipments via the U.S. Gulf. In addition, barge traffic along the Illinois and Mississippi Rivers has been slowed this week due to rising water levels.

The Zen-Noh facility loads about 1.2 million tonnes of grain, mainly corn, for export every month. Industry traders said the company may be able to maintain at least partial operations by loading grain directly from barges or by finding a way to bypass the damaged tower.
Indeed, a few industry brokers said the increased congestion could have the opposite effect in the near-term, pushing rates higher as vessels wait to load their cargo.
"Ships will be on demurrage, costing the charterers a lot more, and creating a scarcity of tonnage in the U.S. Gulf," said a New York-based shipbroker.
Traders said most charterers were likely to prefer relets to other grain elevators when possible, however.
Zen-Noh Grain Corp is the U.S.-based subsidiary of the National Federation of Agricultural Co-operative Associations, Japan's biggest grain importer.
((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
